What you're feeling on day three is very common, and in most cases the milk is actually enough. Mothers often worry about supply in the early days, but almost all mothers can produce more than enough milk if the baby suckles effectively and feeds often (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Usually, even when a mother feels she has too little, her baby is getting what he or she needs (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 120).

Instead of judging by how full your breasts feel, watch two reliable signs: your baby passing urine about six times a day, and adequate weight gain. If urine is small in amount and concentrated, or weight gain is poor, that's when to seek help (MOHFW-IYCF, pp. 81, 120).

Formula now can actually reduce your supply, because babies who get other feeds suckle less at the breast (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). What builds supply is frequent feeding: at least 6–8 times during the day and 2–3 times at night, from both breasts, with good attachment, and no water or other liquids (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62).

If you're unsure, please see your doctor or a skilled breastfeeding supporter to observe a feed — you don't have to work this out alone.

Breastfeeding factors
Delayed start:
If a baby does not start to breastfeed in the first day, his mother’s breastmilk may take longer to ‘come 
in’. This may be the reason for not getting enough milk and starting of weight gain.
Poor support:
If the mothers don’t get immediate support in the healthcare facility for breastfeeding after delivery, 
she usually gets confused and many times gives some other food and fluids to the baby. First time 
mothers find it little difficult to hold and feed the baby. She needs proper support from a skilled 
worker in health facility.
Poor attachment:
If a baby suckles ineffectively, s/he may not get enough milk.
Infrequent feeds:
Breastfeeding less than 8 times a day in the first 4 weeks, or less than 5-6 times a day at an older age, 
is a common reason why a baby does not get enough milk. Sometimes a mother does not respond to 
her baby when s/he cries, or she may miss feeds, because she is too busy or at work. Some babies are 
content and do not show that they are hungry often enough. In this case, a mother should not wait for 
her baby to ‘demand’, but should wake him to breastfeed every 3-4 hours.
No night feeds:
If a mother stops night breastfeeds before her baby is ready, her milk supply may decrease.
Short feeds:
Breastfeeds may be too short or hurried and the baby does not get enough fat-rich hindmilk. 
Sometimes a mother takes her baby off her breast after only a minute or two. This may be because 
the baby pauses, and his mother decides that s/he has finished. Or she may be in a hurry, or she may 
believe that her baby should stop in order to suckle from the other breast. Sometimes a baby stops 
suckling too quickly, for example s/he is wrapped in too many clothes and feeling hot.
Bottles and pacifiers:
A baby who feeds from a bottle or who sucks on a pacifier may suckle less at the breast, so the  
breastmilk supply decreases.
Complementary feeds:
A baby who has complementary feeds (artificial milks, solids, or drinks including plain water), before 
4-6 months suckles less at the breast, so the breastmilk supply decreases.

Congratulations on your little one! While breastfeeding, your body needs extra nourishment — about 600 additional calories and roughly 14–15 g extra protein daily during the first six months (ICMR-) (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 176).

Since you eat eggs, aim each day for:
• An extra meal or snack — a boiled egg, or dal with rice/roti (cereals and pulses in a 3:1 ratio give good protein) (ICMR-)
• Milk, curd or paneer — milk is the best calcium source (ICMR-)
• Seasonal vegetables, green leafy vegetables and fresh fruits; guava or orange with meals helps iron absorption (ICMR-)
• Sprouted or fermented grains (like idli/dosa batter) to improve iron availability (ICMR-)
• Plenty of liquids — water, milk, dal, soup (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 176)
• Iodized salt (ICMR-)

Avoid high-fat, high-sugar and salty foods, and stay away from tobacco, alcohol and other addictive substances (ICMR-, 42). Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets — these are recommended throughout breastfeeding, not just the early months (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 178).

Your little one's first movements, called 'quickening', usually begin between 18 and 22 weeks of pregnancy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 23). At 17 weeks, you're right at the doorstep — so any day now! At first, the sensations may be gentle — like tiny flutters, bubbles, or soft taps — and they can be easy to miss or confuse with gas. Over the following weeks, they'll grow stronger and more distinct.

Later in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester, it's important to be aware of your baby's movements and tell your doctor right away if you notice them reduced or poor (WHO-ANC, p. 54). Executive summary
Introduction
Evidence from a systematic review on antenatal zinc supplementation was evaluated as part of the World 
Health Organization (WHO) antenatal care (ANC) guideline development process in 2016, and the following 
recommendation on zinc supplementation was made: “Zinc supplementation for pregnant women is only 
recommended in the context of rigorous research.” The Guideline Development Group (GDG) made this 
recommendation because it felt that the evidence on the intervention was incomplete and that more research 
was necessary. 
Since the publication of the systematic review, four additional randomized controlled trials have been published; 
therefore, in April 2019, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized the WHO recommendation on 
antenatal zinc supplementation for updating.
Zinc is a trace element found in many foods, particularly in meat, but also in dairy products, legumes and 
unrefined cereals. It plays an important role in many biological processes that contribute to human growth and 
development, and also to immunity. As it is not stored in the body, it needs to be consumed regularly to prevent 
zinc deficiency, which is particularly common in low- and middle-income countries, where dietary intake of zinc-
rich foods is often low. However, the effects of zinc deficiency in pregnancy have not been clearly established.
In January 2021, a WHO-convened GDG comprising most of the 2016 GDG members re-evaluated the evidence 
on antenatal zinc supplementation, updating the recommendation on zinc in accordance with WHO’s living 
guidelines approach.

This suggestion comes from love and tradition, and honey before the first feed is a familiar custom in many Indian families. The health guidance, though, is clear: honey given before your first milk is a "prelacteal feed" (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19), and prelacteal feeds may not be hygienic and can cause intestinal infections in the baby, leading to diarrhoea (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32).

What your newborn needs first is colostrum — your first milk — rich in antibodies and anti-infective factors that protect against newborn infections (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). Breastfeeding should ideally start within one hour of birth, and for the first six months your baby should have only breastmilk — not even water (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32; WHO-POSTNATAL, Rec. 42).

You might share this gently with your mother-in-law — health workers are even advised to talk with mothers-in-law directly (MOHFW-ANC, p. 61). Her care is real; the best first gift is your colostrum. If honey has already been given and your baby seems unwell, please tell your doctor.

Background
Women’s bodies undergo substantial changes 
during pregnancy, which are brought about by both 
hormonal and mechanical effects. These changes lead 
to a variety of common symptoms – including nausea 
and vomiting, low back and pelvic pain, heartburn, 
varicose veins, constipation and leg cramps – that in

pelvic pain, heartburn and varicose veins, often 
worsen as pregnancy progresses.

and worsen with long periods of standing (160).

output.answer: It's lovely that your family is looking out for you — this tradition comes from a place of care. But the trusted guidance I have says the opposite for mothers: India's Ministry of Health postpartum advice is that 'She should bathe daily,' and also wash the perineum daily and after passing stools, change pads every 4–6 hours, and wash hands before handling the baby — all to prevent infection (MOHFW-ANC, p. 61). So there's no need to avoid bathing for 10 days; daily bathing is actually recommended for your recovery and comfort. One thing that may be behind the confusion: the 24-hour delay applies to your baby's first bath, not yours — WHO recommends a healthy newborn's first bath be delayed at least 24 hours after birth, with care to keep the baby warm (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 114). If you had a caesarean, stitches or any complication, I don't have a trusted source about bathing with a wound — please ask your doctor first. Otherwise, a warm (not hot) bath, drying well, and clean clothes should serve you well.

You don't need to bathe your baby every day. You may prefer to wash their face, neck, hands and bottom instead.
This is often called "topping and tailing".

cotton wool and warm water, and gently pat dry with a towel.
It will help your baby to relax if you keep talking while you wash them. The more they hear your voice, the more
they'll get used to listening to you and start to understand what you're saying.

I understand the worry — Bengaluru summers feel hot, and it's natural to think your little one must be thirsty. But for a two-month-old, the answer is no water needed. Your breastmilk has all the water she needs, even in the peak of summer (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). In fact, water is the largest part of breastmilk, and studies show it fully meets an infant's needs even in hot, humid climates (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80).

What helps instead:
- Breastfeed on demand — whenever she cries or seems fussy, offer the breast. Frequent feeds give her both milk and fluids.
- Watch her urine: frequent, pale-coloured urine means she's getting enough fluid (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 149).

Do see your doctor if her urine becomes scant or dark, or if she has fever or diarrhoea — those situations need medical attention, not home water feeds (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 149).

You're doing wonderfully by asking. Trust your milk — it was made for exactly this weather.

Myth #1: Janam Ghuti/Gurti should be given at birth
NO! Nothing can replace the substance produced by your breasts immediately after birth of a

Myth #2: Milk is not enough during the first 3 or 4 days after birth
No, it is not true. During the first few days after delivery, colostrum is produced which is thick, 
sticky and light yellowish in colour. Although secreted in small quantities (30-90 ml), colostrum 
is sufficient to meet the caloric needs of a normal newborn in the first few days of life. It is rich in 
Vitamin A and K which are required by the newborn after birth. With lots of antibodies and other 
factors, colostrum works as the first line of defense against infections.

“breastfeeding”. Some babies fulfill their requirement in 5-10 minutes while other take longer. 
The baby should be allowed to decide the duration of the feed. However, if the duration is 
too long (more than half an hour) or very short (less than about 4 minutes) it means there is a

claims.claim: During pregnancy you actually need to eat more than usual — about 300 extra calories every day — to stay healthy and support your growing baby (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30).
WHO similarly advises a healthy diet with adequate energy, protein, vitamins and minerals throughout pregnancy (WHO-ANC, p. 15).
Going without food or fluids for long hours isn't in line with this guidance.
If you have pregnancy-induced hypertension, restricting fluids or calories can be harmful for the baby (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31).
Sattvik foods like fruits, milk, curd and paneer are all recommended in pregnancy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30).
